title: 1 Hour of Space Marine Lore in Warhammer 40k
fullText: You're about to be born screaming four times over the next hour. Four lives as the emperor's finest. And they all end about how you'd guess. You weren't born. Okay. Of of course you were born. This is Warhammer 40k. Your luck wasn't landing you. Jesus. You were born screaming, covered in blood, and probably already being judged by a servo skull with a clipboard. But that part where you got to be a person, that ended fast because someone looked at your orphaned, half feral 13-year-old self and thought, "Yeah, let's give that kid acid spit and a rocket launcher. First the tests, then the surgery, then the upgrades. They installed 19 organs. Not metaphorically. They literally opened you up and started adding them. One lets you eat poison. One lets you breathe in space. One lets you lick dirt and taste its feelings. Science." Then they stapled the black carropus into your spine, turning your body into a USB port for power armor. From that point on, you didn't wear armor, you were armor. If it itched, too bad. If it pinched, that's loyalty. They erased your name, called it purity. They erased your memories, called it devotion. Your personality, unnecessary variance. You got assigned to a legion, not chosen, assigned to none other than the ultramarines. The blue ones, the noble ones, the ones who print their battle plans on parchment and then light it on fire for extra purity. You didn't feel noble. You just felt heavy. You met your squad in a training cage. No names, just chain weapons and trauma. One of them hadn't blinked in 3 weeks. One quoted scripture in his sleep. One kept talking to his boulder like it was his dead twin. You learn fast because asking questions got you re-evaluated. And re-evaluation meant getting stabbed and replaced by the next kid in line. You were told this was brotherhood. It mostly felt like structured emotional damage. They taught you how to fight before you learned how to eat slowly. They taught you how to chant before you understood half the words. And when your bones broke, good. Now you could learn how to fight while healing. Eventually, you earned your first deployment. Great crusade, they called it. Thousands of worlds reunited with the Imperium. Thousands of cultures that didn't want to be. You were told to bring unity. You brought a bolter and righteous indignation. Your first kill was a rebel who called the emperor overrated. Your second was a child with a plasma gun and too much hope. You told yourself it was for the Imperium. It tasted like burning oil and moral flexibility. You saw your primarch once, Rabbouti Gilman, the avenging son, built like a cathedral and glowing like someone who always files taxes early. He didn't see you. He saw the formation, but you stood straighter anyway. They said he was your gene father. But you didn't feel fathered. Still, you believed in the emperor, in the mission, in the idea that all this pain had a purpose. Because if you stopped believing, even for a second, you might remember what it felt like to be human. And that would be worse. So, you kept marching, kept telling yourself that all is well. And for a while, it actually felt like it was working. The Emperor had a plan. The galaxy had a structure. Your squad only stabbed each other during training drills. Sure, the Great Crusade was mostly yelling and compliance bullets, but at least it was organized yelling. Then your cousin Legion stopped responding to Vox calls. Then another one showed up to a war zone with a new logo and way too much eyeliner. Then someone whispered, "What if dad's just wrong?" And next thing you know, you're getting deployed to remind your own gan brothers what loyalty means with a bolter. You thought the Xenos were bad? Try explaining betrayal to someone who shares your chin structure and war crimes resume. You were promised unity. What you got was cousin on cousin warfare and the galaxy's worst family reunion. One minute you're chanting war hymns with a guy over a ration brick shaped like guilt. The next he's across the battlefield wearing the same armor just slightly moodier whispering about how the emperor isn't who he's used to be. You shoot him in the throat. He doesn't flinch until the second shot. You don't even know if that counts as heresy or just extremely aggressive disagreement. That's the moment the galaxy flips and we call it the Horus heresy. Like branding the end of sanity makes it easier to file. Half the legions go full cult. One primarch stubs his ego and suddenly you're being told to reunite at Bolter Point. Horus betrays the emperor. The council of Naya bans librarians. Nobody checks the math on that. Now every third psyker is auditioning for a warp themed exorcism speedrun. and you're stuck babysitting a chaplain who thinks PTSD is a training opportunity. Your sergeant calls it a civil war. The chaplain calls it divine testing. You just call it Thursday. You're deployed against the sons of Horus. They don't wear Luna Wolf White anymore to see a green and spite. You recognize one of them. You train together on that moon with the servo drones that kept electrocuting people for character. He helped you bury one. You don't bury him. You vaporize what's left, burn the soil, and keep moving. Loyalty used to be simple. Now the wordbearers are quoting scripture midstabbing. The emperor's children turned civilian torture into performance art. The world eaters gave up grammar entirely and now communicate exclusively through chainsaw decibel levels. One guy in your squad starts muttering about visions. He carves something into his armor and calls it decorative. The chaplain calls it a reason to bring out the flamer. You don't ask questions. You just start cleaning your bolter a little more obsessively. They say the siege of terror is coming. that the Emperor will make a final stand, that this is the moment that defines the Imperium. You're not so sure. You're currently kneedeep in dead heretics, guarding a trench that smells like burnt prayer scrolls, watching another Thunderhawk crash like divine satire. You reload. You look across the field and lock eyes with another Estardis. Same gate, same armor, same slightly exhausted posture. You shoot first because if you hesitate, you're next. And just like that, it's no longer about crusades or banners or fate. And before you can catch your breath, the call comes down. Terra is under siege. Time to go home. Or what's left of it. This is it. The final stand. The moment that saves humanity. You're not in the throne room. You're not even near it. You're three decks down, crawling through sewage tunnels beneath what used to be a museum. Above you, titans fighting like kaijuized divorce lawyers. below you and six exhausted brothers bleeding into trench rot and whispering litinies like they're bug repellent. You hold the line for 13 straight days, not because you're brave, because the medicate ran out of stems and figured anyone still moving was fine. You fight through traders, demons, collapsing infrastructure, and your own growing suspicion that maybe this divine plan was more like a group project where everyone died and the emperor took the credit. Then it happens. They say Horus is dead, that the emperor lives. You don't feel victorious. You just feel tired. You clean your bolter again, eat another ration brick shaped like a purity seal, and wait for someone to tell you what's next. Nobody does. The psykers go quiet. The chaplain cries for the first time in his life, and pretend it's condensation. The sky looks wrong. You ask if we won. They say the emperor endures, which is code for he's been stapled to a throne and wired into the psychic mainframe like a divine Wi-Fi router. You don't see his body, but you saw the aftershocks, the silence, the sermons rewritten mid-sentence. The people too scared to ask what alive really means anymore. They say he chose this that he's watching. You look around at the broken wall, the shattered squads, the half-dead world you're now responsible for protecting. But there's no time for grief because the traitors, they're not dead, just running. And the Imperium, it's not victorious. It's about to get rebranded. New banners, new rules, same nightmare. The heresy ends on paper, but the cleanup, that's just getting started. They told you Horus was dead, that the Emperor was alive, that the Imperium stood victorious. Then they handed you a flamer and told you to start with your old recruitment planet. This wasn't about justice anymore. This was about optics. The scouring wasn't a war. It was a cleanup. One by one, you chased the traitor legions into the eye of terror. World by world, monument by monument. If it bore the wrong colors, burn it. If it quoted the wrong scripture, burn it. If it didn't cheer loud enough during a compliance parade, double burn. You asked if this was still holy work. The chaplain stared at you so long you started reciting litinies out of guilt. You're given a fresh purity seal and told to stop asking questions. You pin it to your chest like it's supposed to keep the memories from leaking out. Spoiler, it doesn't. The CEX of Stardies gets introduced with splits legions into chapters to prevent another Horus, trading might for control. Gilman writes it. And by writes, we mean data dumps 500 pages of passive aggressive war rules and calls it divine structure. Your job now includes checklists. You used to charge into battle with a chainsword and a scream. Now you submit a formation request and wait for bolter clearance. You lose your first friend to deviation. He wore his old legion tattoo one day too long. Then say he retired. You find his helmet in the supply bin 2 weeks later. Sometimes in the silence between deployments, you find yourself whispering their names. The ones they made you burn, the ones they made you forget. You say them in low Gothic. Quiet just once, then delete them again. Because in the Imperium, memory is a liability. But paperwork, paperwork is sacred now. And your legion, not a legion anymore. Now it's a chapter. Same colors. Fear brothers. More mandatory war chance. Some of your squad got reassigned. Some volunteered to start new chapters. One vanished mid briefing and came back with a different name and a promotion. No one asked questions. You just called him brother and pretended the old name didn't echo. There were no more glorious crusade charges. Now it's tactical engagement pattern gamma ters. Approved by middle management and blessed by bureaucracy. You used to win battles by instinct. Now you win them by powerpoint. Your captain starts quoting subclauses midfight. Your sergeant carries a purity checklist. You find yourself missing the days when you just punched heretics and prayed after. Your chapter gets a new chaplain. He's younger than your helmet. Quotes doctrine like slam poetry. Calls the emperor the first spreadsheet. You laugh then realize he's serious and then cry a little silently because emotion is still considered a soft mutation. You fight in a dozen more crusades against orcs, Elar, and things so weird the administrative hasn't named them yet. You lose brothers, you gain honors, but you forget what the honors were for. Sometimes you see the others, the new chapters. They share your gene seed, not your memories. You used to feel like a sword. Now you just feel heavier. And I don't mean emotional baggage. Okay, maybe I do. I can't be your narrator and your therapist, so like this one's on you. But hey, that's just aging, right? According to the Codeex, you're still combat effective. And if you're not, well, the Imperium has a plan for that, too. You just get repurposed, so you keep going. Decades blur, wars change names, enemies respawn with new hats, and you you've been at war for centuries, or at least it feels like that. you stopped counting somewhere around your 20th compliance campaign or your eighth crusade or maybe it was that one skirmish where your arm got vaporized and the tech marine reattached it using incense, duct tape, and what might have been fake. Point is, you're still here and honestly, you're starting to think that is the punishment. The galaxy keeps changing. New Zenos, new cults, new ways to scream in languages your auto translator actively censors for morale reasons. You once fought a creature that wasn't born in real space. Your captain called it a demon. You called it Tuesday because Thursdays already got bucked. The warp storms get worse. Time fractures. One mission takes two hours for you, 12 years for everyone else. You return to base and find out your chapter already mourned you, replaced you, and assigned your bunker to a servtor named Clanky. Clanky snores loudly. You fight alongside new recruits now. Primaris, shinier, taller, built like bad decisions and power armor. They're polite, efficient, soulless. You don't hate them, you just hate that they still believe. Your chaplain starts mumbling during sermons. Your apothecary stops naming the dead and starts assigning serial numbers. You haven't prayed in 38 standard cycles, not because you lost faith. You just ran out of new material. Sometimes you dream about your old squad. Sometimes you see them on the battlefield. Problem is, you're pretty sure they've been dead for 400 years. You ask the librarian if that's normal. He says, "Define normal." Then his nose starts bleeding. You reload, you fight, you keep going because you're a space marine. You don't get to stop. You barely remember getting reassigned to this new warp mission. One minute you're patching up a bolter with duct tape and sarcasm. The next you're staring out at a pothole at a space that's technically illegal to look at for too long. Great. Warp travel again. You've done this before hundreds of times. You've got the whole routine down. Recite the lities. Bless the toilet. Don't make eye contact with a bulkhead if it starts pulsing. But this time, no screams, no visions, just vibes. bad ones. You tell yourself it's fine. Maybe the Gellerfield just feels extra cursed today. Maybe it's normal for the medic station to hum in harmony with your heartbeat. Maybe the bolter is supposed to whisper your name when you're not holding it. You ask the chaplain. He tells you the emperor protects. Then forgets your name. Then blesses a vending machine. So you stop asking. Instead, you do what you've always done. Clean your gear. Ignore the walls exhaling like they've got lungs. You start dreaming weird again. Not scary, just familiar. Too familiar. You see old battlefields you don't remember fighting on. Dead brothers saying things you definitely never said, except it still feels like you said them. You chalk it up to stress or time dilation or the emotional equivalent of filing taxes for 900 years straight. The warp doesn't scream this time. It size like it's been watching you this whole time and finally went, "Okay, buddy. You've earned a break." And the worst part, you almost believe it. That the whispering's done. That the worst is over. that you'll finally get to rest. But nope, you wake up to another drop pod, another flame briefing, another heresy. Okay, now you've been fighting for a long time, like long time. You're not sure how long exactly because time has gotten weird. Could be a few centuries, could be brunch. All you know is the bolter still works. The mission isn't over. And some shiny new Promeus just called you ancient like it was a compliment. You keep getting honored. Medals, blessings, spirity seals staple to your chest like divine participation trophies. You haven't taken your armor off in ever, but that's fine. Stardies don't retire. They just get louder when they breathe. Then there's the new guy, wideeyed, fresh jean seed. Looks at you like your history class with a pulse. Says something like, "It's an honor to serve beside you, ancient. What's it like being awake?" You laugh. Except you don't. Your speaker clicks. The kid salutes and walks away thinking he heard divine static. You sit there wondering when your voice stopped working. You chalk it up to warp trauma. Maybe spiritual compression. Maybe the armor is just extra creaky today. You've been through worse. Like that one battle you half remember where your chest blade got split open and your legs stopped working and someone whispered, "We can still use him." Then nothing. Anyway, no time to dwell. There's heresy to extinguish. Mid battle, mid flamethrower burst, you turn toward a shattered wall panel. It reflects just enough light for you to see. A sarcophagus wired up like a cathedral fuse box. Fists the size of jet bikes. Legs bolted to a mech frame. Your frame. Oh. Huh. You're a dreadnot. Okay. Cool. Cool. Cool. Cool. Cool. That explains a lot. The memory gaps, the voice delay, the weird dreams, the fact that you haven't blinked since the Horus Heresy. You were expecting a dramatic reveal. Choirs maybe. Instead, it's just you, your reflection, and the slow realization that you've been kind of dead for 300 years and still not on break. You nod to yourself, or at least the sarcophagus nods. Close enough. You're a space marine. Now you're a very expensive microwave that punches tanks. You weren't born a hero. You were born screaming on a volcanic death world where the air occasionally tries to murder you. Nocturn, where pleasant weather means only three earthquakes today. Your childhood was simple. Learn to forge metal. Don't die in a lava flow. Maybe avoid the alien slavers. Standard stuff. Then at 6 years old, the sky opened. Not metaphorically. The Dukari arrived. Space elves with a concerning enthusiasm for slave taking and recreational torture. They hit easy and fast. Your city didn't stand a chance. People screaming, buildings burning, your neighbor getting dragged toward a ship. You thought, "I'm really going to die before GTA 6." Then crash. A drop pod. Five salamanders stepped out. Green ceramite and coordinated violence. The sergeant grabbed a Ducari by the throat, crushed his windpipe, then pulled a civilian from a burning building. Same hand. Gentle with humans. Delete mode for Zenos, aka anything non-human. Two settings only. When it ended, he looked at you. Red eyes behind a skull helmet. You thought, "I want his job." That's called foreshadowing. He was a hero. Someone who mattered. Someone people looked at with awe. You wanted to be that to save people like he just saved you. Turns out they'd been watching. An apothecary. The chapter's medical guy had been screening kids for years, checking genetics, seeing who might survive what comes next. A chaplain, basically a warrior priest who makes sure you don't go insane, observed the forges, watching who had patience, who hadn't quit. Two years later, the sergeant-at- asks your parents if you could apprentice. They said yes because when an 8-ft tank asks to borrow your child, you don't argue. The forge became your life. Your master didn't talk much. When he did, it sounded like a self-help book. Eventually, he taught you the Prometheian creed, the salamander's philosophy. Self-reliance, solve your own problems, purification through fire, trials make you stronger, unyielding, never retreat. That last one was cultural and genetic. Kind of both. The salamander's gene seed, the biological blueprint that makes them superhuman, didn't make them stubborn. Noctturn did that. The philosophy did that. Some salamanders took unyielding too literally. Some salamanders, your brothers, refused to retreat even when it was tactically smart. Died holding ground because their pride wouldn't let them back down. Your master channeled his inner master Ugay again. We're forged to endure. Sometimes the metal doesn't bend, it breaks. That's the price. You figured the price was worth it. Then your master got deployed. Three brothers left, two came back. A Brander priest pressed glowing iron to your master's chest. Honor scars, marks of my friend is dead and this burn is all I have left. Later at the cremation, his squad thrust their arms into the flames, sharing the heat, sharing the pain. Brotherhood burns. Your master opened the tome of fire, the chapter's philosophical text, and read while you looked at the ashes at the empty space in the formation and thought, "Oh, this job has a mortality rate." Later, he told you why the chapter was small, why every loss hurt. Isvon V. A betrayal during the Horus Heresy, a galaxywide civil war 10,000 years ago. The 18th Legion walked into a trap. 83,000 salamanders. Second wave legions turned their guns on the first. 98% casualties. At 12, your master handed you a data slate. The Pantheon Council approved you. The council chapter leadership had been watching your progress. Gene seed screening came back clean. You didn't quit, and you helped that other kid who burned himself. Self-reliance doesn't mean selfishness. It means solving problems. That's salamander thinking. Your family gathered that night. Yeah. In the story, you don't get the orphan story. They celebrated. Your sister was still hesitant. Asked if you're sure about this. You thought about that sergeant. You wanted to come back as someone who saved people, a hero. You didn't yet know what that will cost. Next morning, you left for Prometheus, the moon where the chapter fortress sits. Your master didn't say goodbye, just returned to his forge and started heating coals. Because that's what salamanders do. They endure, they work, and they don't do feelings before 10:00 a.m. Prometheus was a volcano with a filing system. You arrived with 30 other aspirants. Week one, five disappeared. Administratively relocated, they said, "You didn't ask questions. The surgery started immediately. No consent forms. Just lie down. We're installing a second heart because one heart is for people with low expectations. You wake up feeling like your chest was having an identity crisis. Then they kept going. Bone reinforcement, muscle weaving, glands with unpronouncable names, like someone kept adding DLCs to your body without asking. Between surgeries, they ran combat drills. You're slower than the others. The apothecary explained, "Sam's gene seed does that. Trade off for benefits. Enhanced heat resistance, radiation tolerance, faster healing. You also get fire sight, infrared vision linked to your armor for tactical heat pulse communication. Very useful. Also disorienting when everyone looks like a thermal camera filter. The chaplain pointed at a forge and told you to make a blade. No protective gear channeling Vulcan's trial. Vulcan was your primark. The salamander's genetic father and greatest blacksmith. The forge was surface of a star hot. You swung the hammer. Hours passed. The blade took shape. Ugly. Crooked. Butter knife with ambition. But it was something. The chaplain inspected it and handed it back. Do better. Thanks, Dad. Then the mutation started. Your skin darkened over the years gradually as the gene seed interacted with Nocturn's radiation. Cold black. Every salamander gets it. You caught your reflection and didn't recognize yourself. One aspirin screamed about being a monster. They dragged him away. You looked at your reflection again. Cold black skin, red eyes glowing like warnings. Monster face. But monsters can be heroes if they save people, right? You had to believe that because there was no going back. The chaplain opened the tomb of fire again cuz motivational quotes have been working so well so far. Pain is a hammer. You are the metal. You wanted to believe that. Mostly you just wanted to stop itching. The real test came during the time of trial. An orbital event. Every 15 years, Prometheus swings too close to Noctturn. Gravity gets by ideas. Volcanoes erupt simultaneously. Tectonic plates file for divorce. They handed you a knife and a canteen. Survive 2 weeks alone. 3 days in, you found another aspirant. collapsed, dying. The trial was solo, but you stopped, found safer ground, dragged him to shelter, shared your water. Later, they tested the unyielding. Hold a position for 1 hour. At 59 minutes, the chaplain ordered retreat. You didn't move. Couldn't. You held the full hour, collapsed after. That was stupid, but also very salamander. Years blurred. By 18, your body was unrecognizable. Too big, too strong, too other. But still you probably the final trial. The fire drake hunt solo. Come back with a hide or don't come back. You descended into the lava tubes. Found another aspirin's body. Guess he felt the hunt. You kept moving. The drake found you first. Massive scaled opinions. The fight was desperate. You drove the knife into its throat. It nearly killed you, but it died first. You skinned it. But no, you weren't done yet. The chaplain handed you tools. Forge a shield from the bones and scales. 6 hours. A time craftsmanship test after nearly dying. Very reasonable. You work through exhaustion. Drake bones as frame. Scales for plating. The shield wasn't perfect, but it was yours. The chaplain said. Acceptable. High praise. The brand priest pressed glowing iron to your chest. Your first honor scar. You felt the weight. A forge master presented you with a drake scale cloak, heavy and fireproof. You received your power armor. You were now a salamander. The ship you had immediately. Your first deployment was disaster relief. Not combat, not glory. Cleanup duty. A hive city collapsed. Earthquake or architecture. You arrived as a scout with a boulder and zero training in urban search and rescue. The city was rubble. Your fire site, that infrared vision the gene seed gave you, lit up everywhere. Heat signatures. People trapped hoping someone cares. Surprise, you do. You pulled 17 people out that day. A woman screamed at your appearance. Black skin, red eyes, eight feet of what the fresh hell is this? But once the fear wore off, she was fine. Saving her kid helped a lot with it, too. After that deployment, they moved you up. Full battle, brother. Third company, real armor, real weapons, real expectations. Translation: Now you get to fight, not just watch. When you return to Noctturn, your family celebrated. Awkward. You didn't fit through the doorway anymore. Your sister tried hugging you, like hugging a cereamite statue. She said you'd changed. Understatement of the millennium. Your sister showed you pictures. She had a boyfriend now, talking about moving in together, future plans, normal things. You tried to be happy for her, but you didn't fit in their conversations anymore. She talked about jobs and rent. You talked about pulling people from rubble. She talked about Sunday morning walks, and you talked about kill competitions. Conversation died. You left early. She gets to have a future because you don't. Fair trade has to be. Second deployment, Armageddon. Third war for that cursed rock. Orcs everywhere. Continent sized wag. The usual. Before departure, the brand new priest pressed hot iron to your shoulder. Ritual preparation invoking Vulcan strength. You didn't flinch. Pain is just feedback now. Then your first warp jump. The warp. That nightmare dimension ships travel through where physics goes to die. They activate the Gellerfield. Basically a please don't let demons eat our souls force field. It flickered. The navigator, the mutant whose third eye steers ships through literal hell started sweating. Not a good sign. Ship time 3 days. Real space 5 weeks. Time is now a suggestion and you're not getting overtime. You fought alongside the Marines malevolent. Nice guys. If nice means civilian casualties are feature, not a bug. Their captain suggested orbital bombardment on refugee zones swarmed by Zenos. Apparently acceptable losses. Your captain Tan himself, yes, the chapter master is personally leading this one because Armageddon is that bad. Responded clearly, one shell near civilians. Salamanders returned fire on them. The bombardment didn't happen. Tuchan's body language said, "Try me." They didn't. You held the evacuation route, lost two brothers doing it. The malevolent punched through faster, left thousands of corpses, called it efficiency. At the cremation, your squad thrust arms into the py flames. Your turn. You pushed in, held it there. The pain was overwhelming. You ignored it. Brotherhood burns, literally. Between deployments, you returned to Nocturn. Your sister was married now. Showed you wedding photos. Her husband was normal. Soft hands, nervous around you. She said she'd name her first kid after you. You nodded. Didn't know what to say. You watched them hold hands. Be human together. You were a weapon. Weapons don't get that. But weapons protect people who do. That's the trade. Third deployment. A year later, Dari hit a mining colony in the Ghoul Stars. Raider slave taking operation. Extended warp travel, weeks aboard, months outside. Time dilation was becoming routine. Horrifying routine, but routine. By the time you arrive, they've been added for days. Torture pens everywhere. Civilians still alive, barely. With refugees, you're gentle. With Dukari, deletion protocol. Bolt rounds through spines. Flamers on runners. They screamed. You didn't stop. These were the ones who took your neighbor. Yes, even the six-year-old hiding in the corner. Payback was methodical and involved creative uses of fire. Your captain gave the order, burned their ships, cut off escape. Casualties, everyone aboard, including captives. You raised the multimelta. Fired. The ship went up. You heard the screaming through the vox, through the hole, through your soul. Mission success. Thousands saved. Cost hundreds already captured. The mat checked out. Your conscience didn't. You went to the chapel, opened the tomb of fire, found a passage on necessary sacrifice. Didn't help. Turns out scripture is bad at justifying burning people alive. The chaplain found you staring at the wall and dropped another crumb. We carried the weight so others don't have to. Technically correct, the worst kind of correct. Your sister gets to have grandkids someday because you burn those ships. Those civilians go home to families. You go back to war. That's the cost. That's the choice. You made it. They didn't. Later, the brander priest applied honor brands marks a victory. This scar felt heavier. Now you knew exactly what it cost. Welcome to being a veteran where every achievement comes with trauma. Decades blur. Compliance campaign. Zenos purges. The usual. One deployment on some forge world you'll never remember the name of. Your squad leader takes a plasma bull defending a refugee convoy. You take command. Temporary. Make the calls. Lose one brother. Save 300. They make it permanent. Veteran sergeant translation. Now you sign the death certificates. Major campaign. Multi-chapter deployment. Extended warp travel through routes getting worse. The navigator warns the warps deteriorating. They call it the great rift. A galaxy spanning warp storm that tore reality in half. Right now you just know the gallerfield struggling and things keep looking in. Ship time 4 years. Real space 60 years. The mission. Evacuate an agri world before a chaos warb band reaches it. Standard extraction. Except intelligence was wrong. The enemy is already there. Your company's cut off in the capital city with refugees. Thousands. No way out except through them. 7-day siege. Day five. Your best friend takes a laz cannon blast meant for refugees. Steps in front on purpose. Last words. Into the fires of battle unto the anvil of war. Very poetic. Very dead. But you gave the order that put him there and have no time to dwell on that. Relief arrives. 14 brothers lost. 4,000 civilians saved. Victory. Allegedly. You returned to Noctturn. Decades passed outside. Your sister, gay-haired now, hugs you. Says you look the same. You feel ancient. Her grandchildren stare at you, scared and odd and equal measure. Your sister told them about you. The hero uncle who saves people. Different paths, different costs. She got to grow old. You got to make sure she could. You tell yourself that's worth it. So you force yourself up and go back. You've accepted the weight, ready to keep going. Two more centuries of exactly that. More deployments than you can count. Eventually, Tan summons you. Personal audience. 400 years served. Scars beyond counting. The Pantheon Council agrees. Fire Drake material. First company elite based on Prometheus. Now Tusan's honor guard. Protect the chapter master. Advise when asked. Look intimidating. Facial brands mark centuries of service. Tuchan assigns you to assist the forge father in hunting the spear of Vulcan, one of nine relics hidden before the primarch Vulcan vanished. Prophecy says recover all nine and Vulcan will return. He's a perpetual so dying and coming back isn't weird. You track it for 3 years. Find it in a chaos vault. Kill 17 heretics. Return the spear to the requery. One recovered, eight to go. Before your next deployment, the brander priest brands you again. By now you've lost count of the scars. The mission standard extracts civilians from a hive under chaos assault. Cultists, demons, the usual. Evacuation's nearly done. Then the Vox relays information. Bridge overrun. 3,000 refugees cut off. You're closest. You're in Terminator armor. Not fast, but very durable. You reach the bridge. The scene's bad. Swarm pouring in from both sides. Not metaphorical. Actual swarm. Mutated horror spilling from the hive. Like the world itself's melting. Your brothers are already forming a firing line, but it's not enough. The civilians won't make it across in time. The only way to save them is to destroy the bridge. Problem? You're still standing on it. You order everyone off. Refugees run across. Thousands. Last one's a kid, maybe 6 years old. Looks back through the smoke. You see that look, same one you had, and he see it. You give him a thumbs up like that sergeant gave you. The kid nods, runs. You detonate the support beam. The bridge crumbles. You fall with it. Long way down. Enough time to think. That kid's face. Your sister's grandchildren. Thousands of strangers. You became what you wanted to be. Impact. Bones shatter. Armor splits. Still breathing barely. They find you hours later. Half buried in slag. The apothecary's face says it all. Hours later, Tashan presides over your funeral. The Lavarite full honors. They carry you to the Magnaflow and shattered armor. Drake's scale cloak still attached, held together by spite and stitching. You can't move, can't speak, but you're still here, watching through failing fire sight as they position you over Noctturn's heart. The heat hits even through broken cereamite, overwhelming, familiar. You've been burning your whole life. This is just the last time. The lower you in, your armor glows, melts. You feel the chapter watching. Young salamanders will carry the fire after you. Metal to metal, fire to fire, Noctturn reclaims what it made. And you think as flames take you and consciousness fades, that kid will remember just like you remembered. The flame passes on into the fires of battle unto the anvil of war and also into therapy. Except therapy doesn't exist yet, so mostly just fire. You wake up to your mother singing. She does this every morning. Some old ballite song about water and hope. Your father is teaching you how to shoot. He's been at it for months now, showing you how to check rad sensors, spot the dust storms that roll across balls, secundus, make a kill shot count. You're not very good at it yet. Miss more than you hit. Your mother doesn't like the shooting lessons. Wants you learning the water purifiers instead. Keeping people alive rather than learning to kill. They argue about it sometimes. Not today. Today's quiet, normal. Your father's running parameter checks with the other settlers. Your mother's maintaining the wells. You're supposed to be helping her. Instead, you're still half asleep when the shooting starts. The raiders come at dawn, 12 of them. Your settlement has water, actual drinkable water, which makes it a target. Your father is already shouting for families to reach the caves. He tells you to run. You grab your rifle instead, the one he's been teaching you to use. You reach the perimeter and see a raider 20 m out. Easy shot. Your father's made you practice it 100 times on the range. You miss. The raider doesn't. Your father takes the round meant for you. You're on the ground, rifle in your hands. Hands won't stop shaking. Your mother appears, grabs you, tries to drag you toward the caves. Two raiders cut her off halfway to the caves. She puts herself between you and them, kills one with a scavenge blade, shoves the blade into your hand, tells you to run. You're too slow, too scared, too frozen. You're standing there watching her fall. Someone drags you into the caves. 30 families, 17 make it. You watch from the cave mouth as raiders loot your settlement. Burn what they can't carry. You have a broken knife and rage and the growing understanding that you aren't strong enough. Not strong enough to save them. Not fast enough to reach them in time. Just not enough. The raiders are loading water when the sky opens up. Three warriors in red armor drop from the clouds. They don't slow down. Don't hesitate. 30 seconds later, every raider is dead. One warrior approaches the caves, taller than the settlement's water tower, armor covered in blood and sand. He tells you it's safe. Voice processed through his helmet. Inhuman but not unkind. Blood angels. Post human warriors built to defend humanity. He did in 30 seconds what your parents died trying to do. What you couldn't do at all. He's strong enough to protect everyone. Strong enough that nobody dies on his watch. You want that. The blood angels secure the area. Colin supplies medical aid. A sanguinary priest in white armor tends to the wounded. He approaches, asks if you're injured, you shake your head. If you lost someone, you nod. He says the Blood Angels recruit from Ball that strong young warriors who survive tragedy sometimes find purpose in service. Their fortress monastery holds trials in three days. He looks at you carefully, says you have the eyes of someone who'll either do something great or something terrible, sometimes both. You don't know what that means, but you will soon. You bury your parents that evening. You leave for Arcs Angelicum 2 days later. You're going to become strong enough protect people strong enough that you never freeze again. Whatever it takes. The trial starts immediately. 200 aspirants aed 13 to 17 all from Bal or its moons. A chaplain explains the trials. 3 days in the deep waste reaching Angel's fall. Then arena duels, endurance tests, ritual combats. Only then does the chapter choose who drinks from the grail. For now, survive 3 days. You're given a knife and a compass bearing. That's it. Day one, you walk. The wasteland doesn't care about your grief. The sun's trying to cook you. The sand's trying to bury you. That's fine. You're angrier than the desert. Day two, you find a cave system. Someone's already inside. Maybe 16. Grinning like this is a summer camp, dragging an unconscious aspirin into the shade. He introduces himself as Dino. Says there's room if you want to team up. You ask why he's helping someone who's already unconscious. He shrugs, says he blood angels don't leave people behind. Figures he should practice. You don't point out he's not a blood angel yet. The optimism is kind of working for him. You tell him the unconscious kid's probably dead. Dino says probably doesn't mean definitely. You stay because the cave's real and your lips are splitting and that scorpion outside is absolutely not natural. The unconscious aspirin dies during the night. Dino buries him at dawn. Says a prayer you don't recognize. You ask where he learned it. He says his mother taught him. She's dead, too. Suddenly, the optimism makes more sense. Day three, you wake up to someone new. Cassian. Lean, watchful, knife in hand. Dial tries to welcome him. Cassian cuts him off. Track two aspirants who had water, waited for them to kill each other, then took their supplies. You ask if he helped a survivor. Cassian asks, "Why'd he do that?" Fair point. You ask why he's sharing the cave instead of killing you both in your sleep. He says three is better than one when the mutants come. You didn't know there were mutants. There are definitely mutants. You take position. Three of you survived because Cassian noticed. You don't thank him. He wouldn't know what to do with it anyway. The three of you survived the three days. 147 others don't. They call it insangrination. A sanguinary priest presents the red grail filled with blood that's been mixed with the primarch. Sanguinius's own blood and preserved across generations of the chapter. He explains what happens next. You'll drink. Gene seed will bond with your body. You'll be sealed in a golden sarcophagus while unconscious. Over the next year, you'll undergo 19 organ implantations. Few survive. He doesn't mention the red thirst. Not yet. Dino drinks first. drops immediately. Cassian second goes down like someone cut his power. Your turn. The blood tastes like copper and iron and something electric. Something that recognizes you're hungry for power and whispers that it can help. You dream for a year. When you wake, everything's different. You're bigger, stronger. You can hear Dino's heartbeat three beds over. Smell water running through pipes in the walls. The sanguinary priest is watching you. You ask if everyone feels like this. He says no. Your integration was aggressive. The GNC took to you faster than normal. Bonded harder. That's either very good or very bad. He tells to report any unusual symptoms, any hunger that doesn't fade, any urges you can't explain. You nod. You don't mention that your mouth waters when the surf walks past, that you can smell the cut on his hand from across the room. You're too busy feeling powerful to think it's a problem. They assign you to the 10th company scouts. The three of you end up in the same squad. Dino declares you brothers. Says surviving trials and transformation together means you're bonded for life. Cassian points out that most of your trial mates died in the sarcophagi. Dino says that makes you even more bonded. Cassian doesn't argue. You think he might actually agree. Not full battle brothers yet. That comes after you've earned the black carpass, the final implant that turns your body into a living interface for power armor. Right now you're just enhanced teenagers with guns and supervision. 6 months of training follows. Combat drills, tactics, history. Dino drags you both to the art halls between drills. Says it's chapter tradition. Blood angels create beauty to counter the violence. You think it's stupid until you pick up a brush. The painting quiets something in your head you didn't know was screaming. Dino paints abstract hope. Cassian creates geometric precision. Lifeless angles. You paint your parents strong alive together. With your graduation comes a new shiny red power armor and your first combat deployment. War raiders hitting an agri world, simple suppression, protect civilians, eliminate Zenos. You see Dino excited, Cassian preparing his power sword, and you finally get it, brothers. Your squad drops into chaos. Dino charges forward with his flamer, takes down five orcs before the weapon clicks empty. Three more corner him. He's good. kills one, wounds another. The third raises a power claw. You're moving before thinking. You reach him. Put yourself between Dino and the orc. It's bigger than expected. You're losing. Then you smell it. Dino's blood almost breached at the shoulder joint. Something in your brain lights up like a flare. Your body moves on its own. Mouth on the wound. Just a taste. The power hits instantly. Everything sharpens. The world goes bright and fast. You turn on the orc and tear it apart with your hands. When Clarity returns, Dino's staring at you. You just fed on your brother. He asks if you're okay. You lie. He says you saved him. That was incredible. The powers fading, leaving behind hunger that feels wrong. Deep growing. You tell yourself it was adrenaline gene seed glitch. You're lying, but you save Dion. That's what matters. The Sanguinary Priest explains it after the mission. The red thirst is genetic, built into Blood Angel's gene seed. A flaw inherited from Sanguinius that 10,000 years hasn't fixed. There's another flaw, too. The black rage. Brothers lose themselves entirely, reliving Sanguinius's death, seeing enemies that aren't there. The thirst usually comes first. For most brothers, it's manageable, a craving satisfied with rituals and rations. For some, it's a scream. The thirst wants blood. Consuming it triggers enhanced strength, speed, aggression. The danger is feeding it. Every time you give in, it gets louder. Fall far enough, the rage follows. Eventually, you're just the thing it uses to feed. He assigns you extra monitoring, daily rituals, increased rations. You agree to everything. You don't mention the hunger that wakes you at night. That following blood is becoming instinct. 3 months later, it happens again. You almost didn't stop that time. Almost. Dino pulls you away, grounds you. Cassian watches from 15 m away. His hand never leaves his bolter. You tell yourself you're in control. The thirst is a tool. Cassian stands in the corner, silent, watching. That night, he corners you. Says you're using it, feeding it. It's going to kill someone. Probably you, possibly them. You ask what he wants you to do. Will let brothers die. He doesn't answer. Neither do you. Cassian doesn't report you. Protocol says he should. You promise yourself you'll be more careful. You save your brothers three more times. The thirst gets louder each time. Civilians start appearing in the aftermath. You don't remember killing them. The chaplain calls it acceptable losses. You saved more than you killed. The math works. That's what makes it worse. You know what this is now? The thing that turns blood angels into monsters. You know where it ends. The death company. Black armor, chains, suicidal charges until the rage finally kills you. Or execution. If you can't even serve that purpose anymore, you'll do it again anyway because the alternative is watching brothers die. Never again. 6 years since insanguination. The briefing is routine. Tyrannid Splinter fleet near an industrial world. Small force vanguard organisms. Eliminate them before the main fleet arrives. Should be simple. The intel was wrong. The fleet's three times reported size. Organize led by a warrior form coordinating them like pieces on a board. You hit dirt already struggling. Haven't fed properly in 2 months. Trying to keep your promises. Bad timing for self-improvement. The swarm presses forward. Dionel's flamer clicks empty mid-en engagement. Three hormagants drag him down. You smell his blood before you see him fall. Suddenly, you're 15 again. You too weak to stop it. Not again. Not again. You're moving, ripping Zenos off him. Dino's on the ground, armor breached, bleeding from a dozen wounds. He's saying something, probably joking. You don't hear it. You hear his heartbeat. Smell his blood. The thirst rises like a tidal wave. You kneel beside him to stop the bleeding. Your hands move on their own. The world goes red. Not the useful red, not the controlled haze. This is drowning. You're aware of what's happening. Can feel yourself doing it, trying to stop. You can stop. Dino looks at you eyes wide, not afraid, understanding like he knows this isn't your fault. Like he forgives you already. That makes it worse. You're screaming inside your head, fighting for control. Your body doesn't listen. When you finally wrench yourself away, it's too late. Dionel's still looking at you, but he's not seeing anymore. You hide in the industrial complex ruins. Time fractures hours or days. You find blood on your armor you don't remember spilling. Dionel appears sometimes. The black rage starting to take hold alongside the thirst. Visions bleeding through. Not just Dionel. You see golden wings, a throne room, betrayal. Your mind can't tell what's memory and what's gene seed anymore. Cassian finds you on day three. Stands there, bolter aimed at your chest. You barely feel it. The thirst surges. Your body's moving before you can warn him. You're on him in seconds, faster than armor explains. Stronger than you should be. He fights back. He's good, but you're better. Thirsten enhanced, desperate, lost. You get him down, pin him, claws at his throat. Cassian's looking at you, but suddenly you don't see Cassian anymore. You see Dino. Something breaks. Cassian, your last brother about to die because you wanted to be strong enough. The thirst screams to finish it, but you throw yourself off. Cassion see Tyrannids regrouping 30 m away. The thirst needs violence, needs blood. You give it a target that isn't your brother. You charge claws and teeth and fury and the choice to die fighting the right enemy. The tyrannids hurt you good. They hurt you more better. The third screaming, but you're not turning back. Won't turn back. Gastion watches you tear into the Tyrannids away from him, protecting him. He realizes what you're doing, what you chose. The hive mind decides to make a tactical retreat. The Tyrannids scatter. You scream. This was supposed to kill you. Cassian runs to you. You try to warn him, but your body attacks him first. He attacks the same spot where the Tyrannids hurt you. The hunger finally stops. You always thought that Cassian was better with a power sword than the bolter. You regret not telling him that before, but you know he knew. He then returns to Ark Angelicum alone. The priest says he did what was necessary. Somewhere in the monastery, new aspirants drink from the red grail, making promises, seeking strength. The thirst waits for them, too. It always does. You were born screaming on a backwater angry world where the biggest threat was drought and the occasional crop failure. The kind of place where everyone knew everyone's name and nobody locked their doors because what was there to steal besides bad grain and borrowed hope. Your parents died when you were six in a pirate raid. The kind of random violence that hits backwater worlds when someone with guns decides your planet looks undefended enough. The village raised you after because that's what communities did when a child had nowhere else to go. You had your own little group, too. Kale taught you to fight with sticks and told you stories about being brave. Meera made you laugh when the nightmares came, when you'd wake up crying about faces you couldn't quite remember anymore. Tomos followed you everywhere like a devoted shadow, calling you his best friend before he even knew what that meant. Then the vision started. Actual visions, not dreams or intuition or lucky guesses. You'd see tomorrow's storm 3 days early, next week's accident while eating breakfast. That collapsing barn before it collapsed with just enough time to pull the livestock out. At first, people called it luck, then instinct. Then they started noticing patterns that made them nervous. You learned fast that survival meant hiding it. Growing up, you'd heard stories about psykers, people born with warp powers who could see futures or move things with their minds. The stories always ended the same way. Psykers attracted demons, and demons killed everyone nearby. So, you pretended to be observant, studied weather patterns obsessively, made lucky guesses based on careful analysis that kept you three steps ahead without anyone noticing the steps. Because if people knew what you were, they'd either kill you themselves or wait for something worse to do it for them. At 14, the vision came that changed everything. Warp tainted storm with purple lightning. Your village wouldn't survive it. You saw that clearly. saw everyone you love torn apart by something that wasn't just weather anymore. So, you stopped hiding. You didn't know what you were doing, just instinct and desperation and stubborn refusal to let them die. Stood in the field alone and reached out with everything you had. Felt the storm's anger like a living thing pressing against your mind. It worked. The storm veered away and the village lived. You collapsed in the mud, unconscious for 3 days, and created a psychic flare bright enough to be seen from orbit by anyone with the right sensors. 3 days after you woke up, they arrived. Agents of the Imperium's black ships, vessels that travel the galaxy, hunting for psykers. Black ships collect psychic children for the Emperor, either to feel his throne on terror or to be trained as weapons. One crew member looked at you with red eyes behind a hood and didn't blink for the entire conversation. He tested you with a touch that felt like your mind getting examined like cargo at a checkpoint. You passed the inspection. He spoke to the village elder quietly while you stood there pretending not to understand. The translation was simple enough though. Unbound psykers attract war predators. We can protect your people, but only if the source is removed. They didn't want you for the emperor's throne. You were too strong, too useful for something else. Special training was all they said, which sounded official until you noticed how carefully they didn't call it optional. You looked at Kale, at Meera, at Tomos, at the village that raised you when you had nothing. The math was simple and brutal. You leave or everyone dies with something far worse than a storm shows up. You said you'd go. Kale gripped your shoulder hard enough to bruise, but didn't know what to say. Meera cried and made you a necklace from scrap wire and a purity charm from local tradition. Nothing fancy, just something to remember them by. She begged you to come back and you promised because what else could you do? Thos made you promise out loud three times with a pinky promise like that would make it more likely to actually happen. You promised, you meant it. And it was probably the only time you wished your visions had warned you. The black ship had restraint cells on the lower decks. Other psykers inside, young and terrified and chained like cargo. You understood immediately that this wasn't training. This was collection. They searched everyone before departure. Possessions destroyed under purity protocols that didn't allow for sentiment or exceptions. You thought fast, feigned a psychic episode with seizure symptoms that warp proximity causes in untrained minds. In the connection, you noticed the ship rat, but this one was clever with eyes to aware from warp exposure. You reached out with just a flicker of psychic contact and created a bond unconscious and instinctive. then hid the necklace in its nest deep in ventilation shafts where nobody bothered looking. The rat felt your imprint and guarded it. You thought you were clever enough to hide it and get it later, not knowing you'd never see it the same way again. The ship didn't go to terror like they told the village. It went to Titan, Saturn's moon, where a secret fortress existed that most of the Imperium didn't know about. A place that trained the Grey Knights, demon hunters so classified that even other space marines thought they were myths. The ship entered the warp and you watched the stars disappear through the viewport. The black ship docked at Titan. They separated you from the other psykers. Those went to holding cells for processing. You went somewhere else. A grey knight in silver armor gestured you forward toward the chapter's fortress. The fortress monastery was void, cold, and absolute. The kind of architecture that made you feel small just by existing near it. They stripped you of everything. All possessions destroyed and cataloged as impure materials. You touch the empty space on your neck. Good thing you hid it on the ship. Otherwise, it'll be ash now. They sent you to the Chamber of Trials with 30 other selected psykers. Pass and you become a Grey Knight. Fail and you disappear. Run and you also disappear, just faster. They shot three aspirants the first night for trying. Made everyone watch. The only exit is through the trials or through a bold round. 99% failure rate, though they didn't mention that up front, but you figured it out when aspirin started disappearing. Great recruitment vid should have led with that. You made it through by being smarter than the pain. Predicting tests before they started, analyzing patterns that kept you alive. That cleverness saved you. The same cleverness that hid your powers for years. Then the 666 rituals began, and cleverness stopped mattering. They strapped you to a medical slab in the sanctum of purity. Hypnoindo that rewrote your thoughts during forced sleep. Psychic surgery with prognostic. Grey night psykers who could see possible futures, who carved through your mind to erase the timelines where you failed. Memory extraction that pulled everything out piece by piece while you were conscious and couldn't move. You tried to resist, built walls in your mind, safe rooms for the important things, locked away names and faces, and repeated them like prayers. The prognosticars found your walls immediately. Tore them down with psychic force. Week one in the sanctum. Couldn't remember the village name during a memory test. Month three in the combat cages, couldn't remember their faces anymore. Just three people. Month six in psychic conditioning. Couldn't remember why three mattered. Year one after final trials. Couldn't remember if there was anything to remember. They burned those memories. Left only the path where you survive and never fall. What remained was just instinct. Your problem solving became combat tactics. That protective urge became anti-demon zeal. Nothing conscious left to exploit. Years of surgeries and gene seed implantation and combat drills. They implanted the emperor's gene seed. Not a primarks like other space marine chapters received from their genetic fathers, but the god emperor's own template direct from the source. Made you a better psychic conduit. Silver purity seals beneath your skin. psychic words embedded in flesh. Three other aspirants survived training with you. Guran, Tain, Alex. You formed a squad because that's what survivors did. We protect each other became your motto. You didn't know why it resonated beyond tactical meaning. It just did. You learn what grey knights actually do. Other Space Marine chapters fight aliens and traders. You fight demons, warp entities made of pure chaos that corrupt anything they touch. They twist minds just by being near them. Turn loyal soldiers into monsters through exposure alone. This is why witnesses die. This is why secrecy matters. This is why weakness gets you executed. One corrupted Grey Knight could doom an entire world. You learn the doctrine. No Grey Knight has ever fallen to chaos. Not one, not in 10,000 years. You believed it. You'd make sure it stayed true. First deployment. Demoninfested forge world. industrial planet making weapons for the Imperium. You channel psychic power through your sword, spoke banishment rights in languages that hurt to pronounce, felt the demon unravel as reality rejected it. Then watch your squad execute 200 Imperial Guardsmen who'd fought beside you. They'd seen Grey Knights use psychic powers, witness classified techniques, heard demon true names spoken aloud, secrecy breach, standard protocol. You asked if this was normal. He said witnesses are liabilities. You helped with the executions. Years later, deployment to clear a demon corrupted transport. Routine work until you see a rat eyeing you, almost following you. It ran when it saw you finally noticing. For some reason, you decide to follow it. You found the rat in the ventilation system, impossibly alive from warp exposure, still guarding its nest. You found the same necklace and felt nothing except a faint echo. This meant something once. You rationalized immediately. recovered purity charm worth keeping. You kept it as a focus. You didn't think about it again. You're a fullgrain knight now. Chamber militant of the Order Malas, the Inquisition's demon hunting division. Decades of deployments made your squad legendary. Demon purges across the Imperium were saved before corruption could spread. You were noted for tactical brilliance that buried cleverness, keeping your brothers alive when others squads fell. Your minds linked during combat through the egregor psychic battle link that merged four minds into one. You felt Garand's targeting appear in your head like your own thought. Fain's shields wrapped around all four of you without asking. Alex knew where you'd strike before you moved. Perfect coordination. Then came Armageddon. Industrial hive world producing weapons for entire sectors. Billions of workers. Critical infrastructure the Imperium couldn't lose. Enron manifested. The demon primarch of the world eaters, a corrupted demigod, three stories tall, leading an army of berserkers. Your chapter deployed in force. The battle took weeks. You spoke banishment rights while standing in corpse piles. Angrron fell, dragged back into the warp, screaming, "Victory!" The forges survived. Then came the math. Billions witnessed demon manifestation. Billions saw Grey Knights fight. Exposure to greater demons leaves psychic taint in witnesses minds. Corruption spreads like disease. One infected worker goes home, spreads it to his family. The infection grows until decades later, the entire hive summons demons. The order? Purge the population. All of it. You spent months executing civilians. Efficient, methodical. The Space Wolves showed up halfway through another loyalist Space Marine chapter. They called a genocide. Started killing grey knights to stop it. Space Wolves lost. The purge continued. The planet got repopulated later with fresh workers. Guran said approved doctrine works. Fain didn't talk for weeks. Alex kept asking if they'd been right. You didn't question it. You'd seen what demon corruption does. Then thing started slowing down. You noticed during training.3 seconds late, the Agregor Link stuttered. That's how you knew he was done. Milliseconds in reaction time, but milliseconds kill in demon combat. He'd pushed too hard during a banishment, burned out a psychic reserve, saving the squad. Apothecaries, the chapter's medical specialist, confirmed, psychic exhaustion, not corruption. Recoverable with rest. Temporary weakness. Temporary. Grey knights don't do temporary. Verdict: Weekend nights are liabilities. Honorable termination recommended. They knelt and accepted it. Gon froze. Started saying something about brotherhood. You didn't freeze. Demons don't wait. You executed him clean. The agregor linked to like losing a limb you didn't know you had. Garan commented on your lack of hesitation. Hesitation kills. He understood that something in Garan shifted that day. Months later, he was seeing weakness everywhere. Executing problems before they existed. During deployment, Alex showed fatigue and Garan killed him operation without consultation. He realized Garan's paranoia was more dangerous than Fain's exhaustion ever was. The prognosticars agreed. Psychological imbalance, operational liability. You received the order. Garan was waiting in the training cages. He knew. Asked you to do it before he failed. Before he became the thing he'd been preventing. You raised your blade. For one microcond, something flickered. This feels wrong. Conditioning crushed it. You executed the rock. You touched the necklace and felt nothing except familiar weight. You almost threw it away later, almost questioned why you kept it, but it helped you focus. That was reason enough. Your next deployment orders didn't include a planet name you recognized, just coordinates and threat assessment. Major demon incursion, greater demon of ciech, chaos god of change and lies, chaos cult summoning ritual in progress. Standard work, the kind of thing you've done a hundreds of times. You arrive to a world burning with purple lightning, arcing between clouds that moved wrong. The cult had opened a doorway using an old warp scar as anchor. Decades old and festering. The scar registered on your psychic senses like a beacon. And when you scanned it deeper, the signature matched yours perfectly. The greater demon manifested. Bird shaped and crystalline, made of lies and broken futures, it spoke directly into your mind, mocking you for returning to the beacon you'd created decades ago. The wound you'd left when your power screamed from this place. Apparently, demons love monologuing. It's like their only personality trait besides murder. You'd never been here. The village was half destroyed, caught between cultist attacks and demon manifestation, but survivors were still fighting. Your hand went to the necklace unconsciously, the way it always did during psychic strain. You didn't understand the thought or where it came from or why these strangers would matter to you specifically. Now you do. Your training snapped into place like a vault slamming shut. Demonic emotional manipulation. The tug was false nostalgia planted by Zech. The faces were warp spawned illusions. The sense of connection was corruption attempting to find a way in. Your tactical analysis ran automatically. The civilians had been exposed to a greater demon's direct presence for hours. They also witnessed Grey Knights which was a secrecy breach and the warp scar originated from this exact location which made them ground zero for contamination. They were vectors for taint whether they knew it or not. So you would protect them from taint from what they'd seen from what they could become. You authorized the purge. The psychic tug vanished. Just silence where something had been pulling before. Demon tainted all along. Emotional resonance trying to create an opening for corruption. Your squad channeled the right of exorcism. You spoke the demon's true name, forbidden knowledge carved into your mind during the 666 rituals, and watched the creature unravel as reality rejected it. The warp scar sealed shut. Mission successful, threat eliminated, witnesses purged, secrecy maintained. The village burned behind you as standard purge protocols turned everything to ash. You stood watching the flames consume what was left and pulled the necklace from your armor. You walked toward the fire and held it over the flames. Let go. You watched it burn and felt nothing except the satisfaction of proper procedure followed. No time to dwell. Next deployment orders already waiting in the gunship's data slate. The Great Rift tore the galaxy in half 3 years ago. Black ship stopped arriving. No new psykers meant no new recruits. Chapter strength hemorrhaging. You hear they're raiding loyal chapters now, stealing their librarians, hiding the evidence. You'll probably get that order next. And you'll follow it because you always do. Because this is all you are. There's nothing left.
fullTextVi: Bạn sắp được sinh ra và la hét bốn lần trong một giờ tới. Bốn cuộc sống tốt nhất của hoàng đế. Và tất cả đều kết thúc theo cách bạn đoán. Bạn chưa được sinh ra. Okay. Tất nhiên là bạn đã được sinh ra. Đây là Warhammer 40k. Vận may đã không đến với bạn. Chúa Giêsu. Bạn sinh ra đã la hét, người đầy máu và có lẽ đã bị phán xét hộp sọ servo với một clipboard. Nhưng phần bạn phải trở thành một con người đã kết thúc nhanh chóng vì ai đó nhìn đứa trẻ 13 tuổi mồ côi, nửa hoang dã của bạn và nghĩ, "Ừ, hãy cho nhổ axit và một bệ phóng tên lửa. Đầu tiên là các xét nghiệm, sau đó là phẫu thuật, sau đó là nâng cấp. Họ đã lắp đặt 19 cơ quan. Không phải ẩn dụ. Họ thực sự đã mở mang bạn ra và bắt đầu thêm chúng. Một là cho phép bạn ăn chất độc.
